en.title: Resident Evil 2026 Delivers a Joyful, Gory Ride Fans Crave
en.summary: Forget grim survival horror; the latest Resident Evil film is a hilariously gory thrill ride that understands exactly what fans want. Director Zach Cregger unleashes a blood-splattered adventure that prioritizes fun over grit.
en.body:
The world of survival horror is often painted in shades of dread and desperation, but a new contender has arrived to splash it with vibrant, unashamedly sticky red. **Resident Evil (2026)**, directed by **Zach Cregger** and co-written with **Shay Hatten**, isn't interested in being a gritty, meticulously choreographed action flick. Instead, it offers a *joyful* blood splatter of a movie, a 90-minute thrill ride that understands the potent combination of tension, relentless monsters, and laugh-out-loud absurdity.

The film centers on a courier, played by **Austin Abrams**, tasked with a high-priority late-night delivery into Raccoon City. What follows is a descent into a grotesque biomedical outbreak, where mutated humans and relentless infected stand between him and his destination. This isn't a story about a hardened soldier or a brooding anti-hero. Our protagonist is endearingly inept, completely in over his head, and his reactions are precisely what a normal person would have: he messes up, he runs, he makes a lot of jokes about the sheer insanity unfolding around him.

This approach is precisely why **Resident Evil (2026)** works so effectively. Cregger and Hatten masterfully plant seeds of tension, and the payoff is never predictable. It could be a heart-stopping jump scare, or it could be a moment of pure, unadulterated dark comedy. The effects have a satisfying weight to them; the blood feels *sticky*, and the monsters are genuinely unsettling in their relentless pursuit. "There’s a tiny sliver of a plot, but Cregger and Hatten never let it get in the way of a good time," notes one early assessment, and this commitment to pure entertainment is its greatest strength.

## A Refreshing Take on the Franchise

For fans who have followed the **Resident Evil** saga across games and previous adaptations, this film offers a welcome departure. While some iterations have leaned heavily into gritty realism or complex narratives, **Resident Evil (2026)** embraces the inherent B-movie charm of its source material. It’s gross, it’s chaotic, and it’s *hilarious*. The film doesn't shy away from the over-the-top violence that has become a hallmark of the franchise, but it injects it with a self-aware energy that makes it thrilling rather than gratuitous. This is the kind of adaptation that understands that sometimes, the best way to survive an apocalypse is with a healthy dose of dark humor and a shotgun loaded with shells found in an abandoned farmhouse.

## What's Next for Raccoon City's Nightmares

With **Resident Evil (2026)** now unleashing its particular brand of mayhem, fans are already buzzing about what’s next. While specific details about future installments or expansions of this particular continuity have not yet been announced, the film's success is likely to pave the way for more entries that embrace its unique blend of horror and comedy. For now, audiences can revel in this bloody, 90-minute thrill ride that delivers on its promise of pure, unadulterated fun.

Resident Evil is fun as hell, and it’s fun because Zach Cregger and writer Shay Hatten understand how to create tension, plant seeds, and pay that tension off—and you don’t know if the payoff is going to be a jump scare or a gag until it happens. Which is why it works every single time in this movie. This movie is gross, the effects have weight, the blood is sticky, the infected monsters are relentless. There’s a tiny sliver of a plot, but Cregger and Hatten never let it get in the way of a good time. I also have to say up front that this movie is hilarious . If you’re looking for grittiness, or meticulously choreographed action sequences, this is not the adaptation for you. Our main character is inept and in over his head, just trying to get through a night from literal hell. He comments on a lot of the insanity around him because that’s what a normal person would do. He messes up a lot, runs away from fights, does stupid shit, and I was glued to the screen. Or should I say I was absorbed into a roiling mass of infected revenants, like some sort of H.R. Giger version of Katamari Damacy , and I enjoyed every second of it. Before we go any further I need to make a request: Could everyone please stop waving their hands at the movie screen? This seems to be a post-pandemic thing, but every time—and I mean EVERY. SINGLE. TIME.—I go to a movie now, someone is in the theater waving and pointing at the screen like they think the moving pictures on that big wall up there will see them and respond. At last night’s showing of Resident Evil , was it endearing when the girl next to me made grabby hands during the previews, indicating which movies she wanted to see? Yes . Was it increasingly less endearing each time she threw her hands up in exasperation at the terrible decisions made by Resident Evil ’s terrified protagonist? ALSO yes . (And to be clear, this isn’t a generational thing—I have seen people from teens on opening night all the way up to elderly Manhattan Mid-Day Matinee-Goers waving and pointing like they’re at a goddamn rodeo.) With that out of the way.
